chapter_theme: Songs at Thiruvannamalai (திருவருணை, 3 of 6): the poet confesses embraces bought from courtesans whose love lasts as long as the money, the body's foulness and the ruin of old age, and asks for Murugan's feet; two songs speak for a girl sick with love; the praise centres on the tower and hill of Arunai, Murugan as Siva's guru, and stories of Siva for his devotees.
structure_note: Courtesan and lovemaking songs (398, 403, 407, 408, 410, 412), of which 403 vows not to forget the feet even in the embrace; the body as a foul vessel (402); a yogic plea (405); short prayers for grace and steadiness (399, 400, 401); love-laments in a girl's voice or about her (404, 406, 411); and 409, praise alone.

398.reading: The poet describes at length the act of love with women who sell themselves, two bodies becoming one form, hair loosened, bangles jingling, lips drunk, until mind melts into mind, and names them women of magic arts who cling only as far as the money goes; he asks for grace to be let go from them. The praise tells how Murugan circled the whole sea-girt earth in an instant and came to sit at Siva's side, names Palani, Swamimalai (ஏரகம்), Thiruvavinankudi, Brahmapuram and Thiruttani, calls him the one who became kin to the poet, a dog, and made poems, and ends at the north side of Arunai's great tower.
398.nuance: பொருளது அளவும் மருவுறு மாய வித்தை விலைமாதர்: the embrace lasts as far as the money does, which is why the long love scene ends in a plea for release. படியை முழுதும் ஒரு நொடியே மதித்து வலமாக வந்து சிவனிடத்து அமர் சேயே: circling the earth in a moment and sitting by Siva has the details of the contest for the fruit, though no fruit is named. நாயெனுக்கும் உறவாகி நின்று கவிதையைப் புனைவோனே may refer to the poet's own call to sing; the split of these words is unsure.

399.reading: The poet, who speaks the threefold Tamil of verse and song night and day, asks Murugan to give him clearly a settled firmness and his holy grace. The praise names him the great life of supreme compassion, the knower of the truth of Parasiva, and the good son born of Hara's grace, at Arunagiri.
399.nuance: திரம் அதனைத் தெளிவாக: what is asked is steadiness, not release or vision; the poet already sings, and wants the singing to stand firm.

400.reading: The poet seems to say that amid the praises of sages, Brahma, Vishnu, the gods and the devotees, his lone servant's cry goes unheard, and asks whether anyone will speak kindly for him; he wonders what the dust of Murugan's feet and his store of grace are. The praise names him the supreme guru who moves in the atom, who has the elements from wind onward for his army, who is all forms and the ancient form, who threw the vel on darkness when Vishnu and Brahma cried for refuge, and the one at Arunagiri who powders his servant's cruel disease.
400.nuance: அணுவில் அசைவாய், சகல வடிவாய், பழைய வடிவாகிய: Murugan as the mover within the atom and as every form is the doctrine of pervasion, unusual in so short a song. The opening (இருவர் மயலோ அமளி விதமோ) may instead describe love's confusion; how its words split is unsure.

401.reading: The poet asks Murugan to come quickly before him on the peacock, face blossoming and pouring grace, dancing, while the two deeds take fright, the kinds of impurity and the dark disease fade, bees hum at the kadamba and the gods shower flowers calling him the elephant-faced one's younger brother. The praise names Siva, who burned the three cities and Kama's body with a smile, rides the bull and dances in the open space of Sivam with the queen at his side, as the one whom Murugan delighted as guru, and ends with the bed of the hunter girl at Arunai.
401.nuance: The plea is for the sight of Murugan arriving, and the release from deeds and malas is the effect of that sight, not something earned first. சிவம் வெளி அங்கண் ... நடம் செய்து: Siva's dance is placed in the space that is Sivam.

402.reading: The poet names the body a fresh bag fed by the two deeds, a bent nest grown in the womb, a ruined hollow of trouble, a pot where stench and liquor pool, a corpse that sleeps at night, a vessel shaped for pain and a hut that heart and life move out of; and asks whether, giving up the delusion he shared with the world that it will not perish, he will reach Murugan's two lotus feet. The praise names Arunai, where the gods crowd to worship, Vishnu of the Sarnga bow who swallowed the worlds as uncle, Murugan as son of the lord of dance whom the serpent king and another devotee beheld, and the lord of Indra with the vajra.
402.nuance: The confession is a chain of names for the body, each a container (பை, குடம்பை, பொதும்பு, கும்பம், பாண்டம், கூண்டு, குரம்பை), so the point is that what the world takes as lasting is a vessel to be left. உரகேந்த்ரர் கண்ட கடவுள் நடேந்த்ரர் probably means Nataraja as seen by Patanjali, the serpent king; the other devotee (ம்ருகேந்த்ர அன்பர்) may be Vyaghrapada, but the epithets are hard to divide.

403.reading: The poet describes the act of love, hair loosened, sweat like pearls on the face, eyes rolling, garments slipping, lips drunk, until speech fails and the self is lost in desire, and says that even then he will never forget the lotus feet that sages and gods worship, melting. The praise names Murugan the child given by the old knower of the Veda who came in an old man's form to a young man's wedding, pushed in at the gate, claimed him before the assembly as his slave, and stood shaking and protesting when the youth tore the old palm-leaf deed; it also names Vishnu who churned the sea for nectar, the cock on the banner, and the tower of Arunagiri.
403.nuance: The plea is not to escape the embrace but to keep the feet in mind within it (விடுபோதும் ... பாதபத்மம் என்றும் மறவேனே), a different stance from the songs that ask for release from women. The story in the praise has the unmistakable details of Siva claiming Sundarar as his bondsman at his wedding, with the slave deed (ஆவணம்) torn before the assembly; that the god of the story is the giver of Murugan makes Siva himself the claimant of a servant.

404.reading: In a girl's own voice: the pearls on her breasts and the moon that spits fire, the flute's music that comes like the sun to take her life, the sea's waves and Kama's cruel arrows torment her, and she asks Murugan to come in time to the hill at Arunai with its gem-strewn groves so that she does not perish. The praise names him the guru of Siva who burned the three cities with a smile, the hero on the emerald peacock who powdered the asuras, the chest marked by the hunter girl's breasts, and the one who sent the vel to the seven seas.
404.nuance: Akam love poetry in the first person (எனது உயிர், எளியெனும்), not the poet's confession. The torments are the classical ones of evening: moon, flute and sea.

405.reading: The poet asks whether, instead of raising the body's fire like a forge to strike the moon so that nectar melts and flows and he reaches the supreme bliss longing for Murugan's feet, he will wander ashamed like a thief, caught in the net of infatuation with women of bow brows and pearl smiles. The praise names the vel let fly from the golden peacock to drums, the one who was death to the race of the wicked Jains, the one dwelling on the hill of Arunai in the sea-girt land, and the one who cut down the asuras, freed the gods and set up their rule.
405.nuance: உலையில் அனல் ஒத்து ... உடுபதியை முட்டி அமுது ஊறல் உருகி வர: the inner fire raised to the moon so that its nectar flows is the yoga of the Tirumanthiram, set here against the women. கதவு அமணர் உற்ற குலகாலா again makes Murugan the Sambandar who destroyed the Jains.

406.reading: A voice, perhaps the girl's mother or friend, asks whether the vanji-creeper girl of field-rich Arunai should suffer from the moon rising over the sea's waves, the evening and the talk of the gossiping women, and the south wind that scorns even the undersea fire. The praise names Murugan the hero whom Siva, who married Uma at his left, worships, the vel that split the seven hills, the lord who routed the asuras, and the master of Vishnu, Brahma and Indra.
406.nuance: The speaker is not named; வஞ்சி போதநலங்கலாமோ speaks of the girl in the third person. மலந்தைமார் sounds like the blaming women of akam poetry; the word is unusual.

407.reading: The poet paints a woman from lotus face, crescent brow and carp eyes to pearl teeth, areca neck, breasts like pots, creeper waist and peacock gait, and asks whether he should be kin to those who coax a man and snatch his wealth. The praise is a battle in drum syllables, the vel that feeds the demons on the asuras' flesh, and Murugan who went to the millet field and embraced the hunter girl in stealthy love, at Arunagiri.
407.nuance: குனகி பொருள் பறிபவர்: the whole catalogue of beauty ends in two words, coaxing and robbing, so the portrait is a lure. The praise closes on Murugan's own களவு with Valli, stealth in a good sense against the women's theft.

408.reading: The poet heaps conceits on women's breasts, which defeat the lotus bud, the bubble, the golden pot, the tender coconut, the elephant's tusk and the chakravaka bird, and asks whether he should be kin to these thieving women with painted breasts. The praise is a battle in drum syllables with ghouls feasting and the peacock dancing in asura blood, and names Murugan the true guru made manifest on the green steed, who appeared at Arunai and gave the poet clarity.
408.nuance: திருடிகள், thieves, carries the charge. In the praise, மெய்ப்ரத்யக்ஷ நற்சற்குருபர ... அருணையில் சித்தித்து எனக்குத் தெளிவருள் makes Arunai the place where the guru appeared to the poet himself. The comparisons in the first half are dense and some, such as the burning of Kama's crown, are hard to place.

409.reading: A song of praise without a plea: it names Ganapati, the elephant-faced one who destroyed the elephant-faced asura and holds gram, sesame, lentils, plantains and many fruits in his belly, and Murugan his younger brother who fought the asuras and their hill with the vel. It names Siva who held the reins and led jackals as horses, who dances everywhere and wears the flayed elephant's hide, and ends with Saravana of the bright vel at Arunai of rich fields and pools.
409.nuance: நரிமிகுக் கிளைகளைப் பரியெனக் கடிவளக் கையில் பிடித்து எதிர் நடத்திடும் ஈசன்: the jackals turned into horses are the story of Siva acting for Manikkavasagar, a devotee's story in the praise of Murugan's father. The list of foods follows Ganapati's offerings in the opening songs.

410.reading: The poet piles up what women's eyes do: they widen and speak, work Kama's tricks, rival golden earrings, spread like the sea, glow with poison, meet arrows, wage war on the young, wander in stealth and deceit and defeat the humming bee, and he asks whether he will escape being ruined under women who embrace with bewildering eyes and wring out a man's life. The praise shows Murugan walking, his anklets ringing and his flower feet aching, in a changed form among lions, bears and tigers to the millet field, bowing at the hunter girl's small feet and embracing her, then destroying the asuras and dwelling at Arunai on the south side.
410.nuance: Each pair of verbs ends -வன (அகல்வன புகல்வன, கடியன கொடியன), a list of what the eyes do that sounds like a list of beasts. The praise reverses it: the god himself goes in disguise and bows at a woman's feet (சிறு பதயுக சததளம் பணிந்து).

411.reading: A voice laments that a girl, tormented by the distant sea's roar in her ears, by Kama and by the moon, her garment slipping on her bed of flowers, reviled by the townsfolk and the subject of many slanders, should wilt and faint day after day. The praise names Murugan the lord of Sonachala with twelve shining shoulders, whose unfailing vel destroyed Sura, the chest dear to the daughter of the heavenly world, and the master of the gods.
411.nuance: நாடோர்கள் ஏச ... நானா பவாதம்: gossip and slander are part of the girl's suffering, as in akam poetry. The second line (காலாளும் வேளும் ஆலால நாதர் காலால் நிலாவும் முனிந்து) is hard to divide, and who is speaking is not said.

412.reading: The poet describes courtesans who dance in the street and charm for love of coin, wasting some days with them until wrinkles come, then the body's ruin: disease, a staff, walking like a monkey, phlegm, lying on a mat, eyes changed, ears deaf, pain and pleasure forgotten, while townsfolk, kin, wife and children crowd round saying 'chi, this curse won't go'; he asks whether he will fade like that. The praise names Siva who burned Kama and the three cities and drank the poison, and Uma, Vishnu's sister and the poet's mother, who bore the great Kumara of wisdom; the vel dances as Sura, Meru, the seas, the mountains and the serpent's hoods are shaken; Murugan dances on the head of the Veda, and Arunachalam is the pillar of light that ran up and touched the sky.
412.nuance: காசாசைச் செயலாலே: the women's charm is for coin. The kin's verdict (சீசீ சிச்சிசி போகா நற்சனியன்) is the bitter end of the courtesan's life, and the song gives it in their own words. தூணோடிச் சுடர் ஆகாசத்தை அணைந்து: the hill as the column of fire that rose to the sky recalls the Annamalai story of Siva's endless form.

links.note: Both make the courtesan's love last exactly as long as the money: the Naladiyar's lamp goes out with its oil, and 398's women of magic arts cling only as far as the wealth goes (பொருளது அளவும் மருவுறு).

Both call the body a pot (கும்பம்) of filth: the Naladiyar's pot seeps through nine openings under its dark skin, 402's is a pot where stench and liquor pool. The Naladiyar turns the image on the desired woman; 402 turns it on the poet's own body.

Both describe the embrace in full and then refuse to forget the feet within it: 403 says 'even then I will never forget', 420 asks 'even in union, will I forget your golden feet?'. Unlike most of the book, they ask for remembrance, not escape.
Both use the evening torments of love, the moon and Kama's arrows, for a girl in love with Murugan. In 24 her mother speaks; in 404 the girl herself asks him to come before she dies.

Both describe the same yoga: kindling the fire and raising it until the nectar of the moon is drunk. Tirumular calls those who do it Siva-yogis; 405 confesses that the poet has not done it and wanders after women instead.
Both list the foods Ganapati takes, gram or dal, sesame, plantains and other fruits; in 2 they lead into the poet's call to sing, in 409 into pure praise.

Both show the old man with failing speech and a staff. The Naladiyar's still keeps his eyes on desire; 412 follows the man spent on courtesans to the end, deaf and on a mat, while his own wife, children and kin call him a curse.

source_issues: Song 398: line 12 begins with four dots (....) instead of six; harmless.
Song 411: நாடோ ர்கள் (line 6) has a stray space inside the vowel sign; read நாடோர்கள்.
Song 412: நிறா யுற்றிட (line 25) has lost a vowel sign; probably நீறாயுற்றிட ('turned to ash').
